data.tie_meaning: the two members follow each other in the customer community

how_to_read: A density of 0.05 means that 5% of all possible ties between members exist.
The fewer steps lie between members, the faster news can travel through the network.
warnings: The network falls into 6 separate parts (5 of them are members without any tie). A message cannot travel from one part to another.

measures.label: Degree
measures.meaning: The number of ties of a member. Who has many direct contacts?

measures.label: Betweenness
measures.meaning: How often a member lies on the shortest way between two others. Who connects parts of the network that would otherwise be far apart?

measures.label: Closeness
measures.meaning: How few steps a member needs to reach all others. From whom does news travel fastest through the whole network?

measures.label: Eigenvector centrality
measures.meaning: Whether a member is tied to members who are well connected themselves. Who has important contacts, not just many?

centrality_how_to_read: The four measures often agree on who is important. The interesting members are those where they do not.
A member with few ties but a high betweenness is a bridge: the only way between two groups.
centrality_warnings: The network falls into 6 separate parts. Eigenvector centrality then mostly describes the best connected part, and closeness is lowered for members who cannot reach everybody.

how_to_read: Members of one community hear the same news from the same people. To reach the whole network, each community needs its own start.
The communities are found from the ties alone. Compare them with what you know about the members (town, age, interests) to give them a name.
warnings: 5 member(s) form a community of their own, mostly because they have no ties.

forecasting.label: How the Bass model is estimated
forecasting.what_it_does: Decides how p, q and the market potential m are worked out from the sales so far.
forecasting.when_to_choose: Keep the default. Use the regression to see the classic method, or to repeat it by hand in a spreadsheet.

options.label: Nonlinear least squares
options.what_it_does: Tries values of p, q and m until the Bass curve is as close as possible to the sales of every period. Also tells how precisely each value is known.
options.when_to_choose: Default. It is the more accurate method, above all with few periods.

options.label: Regression (the classic method)
options.what_it_does: Explains the sales of a period by the buyers so far and their square, with an ordinary regression. p, q and m follow from the three regression numbers.
options.when_to_choose: You want the method of the original Bass article, or a calculation a spreadsheet can repeat. With few or noisy periods it can fail to give a valid market potential.

forecasting.label: Market potential (m), if known
forecasting.what_it_does: Fixes the number of buyers the product will ever reach. Only p and q are then estimated from the sales.
forecasting.when_to_choose: Leave empty to estimate m from the sales. Enter a number when you have a better source, such as a survey, or when the sales have not yet passed their peak: before the peak the data say little about m.

forecasting.label: Periods to forecast
forecasting.what_it_does: How many periods after the last period of data the forecast covers.
forecasting.when_to_choose: As far as you need to plan. The further ahead, the less certain the forecast.

forecasting.label: Size of the what-if change
forecasting.what_it_does: The forecast is repeated with p, q and m each raised and lowered by this share, one at a time. 0.2 means plus and minus 20%.
forecasting.when_to_choose: Keep 0.2 for a first look. Choose a larger share when you are very unsure about a value.

forecasting.label: Periods per year
forecasting.what_it_does: Published values of p and q are per year. With 4, the forecast is made per quarter: p and q are divided by 4, which gives the same curve in smaller steps.
forecasting.when_to_choose: 1 for a forecast per year, 4 per quarter, 12 per month.

forecasting.label: Numbers of periods to try
forecasting.what_it_does: The Bass model is estimated several times, each time from the first periods only: for example from the first 4, then the first 6, 8 and 12.
forecasting.when_to_choose: Keep the default to see how the estimate settles as more data arrives.

forecasting.label: Forecasting method
forecasting.what_it_does: The rule that turns the sales history into a forecast.
forecasting.when_to_choose: Pick the method that matches the pattern of the series. If you are unsure, let the comparison of methods decide.

options.label: Moving average
options.what_it_does: The forecast is the average of the last few periods.
options.when_to_choose: Sales move around a stable level, and you want a method anyone can check by hand.

options.label: Simple exponential smoothing
options.what_it_does: The forecast is an average of all past periods in which recent periods count more than old ones.
options.when_to_choose: Default. Sales have no clear trend and no season.

options.label: Exponential smoothing with trend
options.what_it_does: Follows the level and the trend of the series (Holt's method). The forecast is a straight line.
options.when_to_choose: Sales rise or fall steadily, without a season.

options.label: Exponential smoothing with trend and seasonality
options.what_it_does: Follows the level, the trend and a repeating pattern over the year (the Holt-Winters method, additive form).
options.when_to_choose: Sales repeat a pattern every year. It needs at least two full seasons of data.

forecasting.label: Periods in the moving average
forecasting.what_it_does: How many of the last periods are averaged.
forecasting.when_to_choose: Few periods follow changes quickly but jump with every random swing. Many periods are calm but slow.

forecasting.label: Periods per season
forecasting.what_it_does: After how many periods the seasonal pattern repeats.
forecasting.when_to_choose: 12 for monthly data, 4 for quarterly data, 7 for daily data with a weekly pattern.

forecasting.label: Weight of the newest period (alpha)
forecasting.what_it_does: How strongly the level follows the newest period, between 0 and 1. Close to 1: the forecast jumps to the latest sales. Close to 0: it changes slowly.
forecasting.when_to_choose: Leave empty: the value that would have forecast the past best is then used.

forecasting.label: Weight for the trend (beta)
forecasting.what_it_does: How quickly the trend is updated, between 0 and 1. With 0 the trend never changes.
forecasting.when_to_choose: Leave empty: the value that would have forecast the past best is then used.

forecasting.label: Weight for the season (gamma)
forecasting.what_it_does: How quickly the seasonal pattern is updated, between 0 and 1. With 0 the pattern never changes.
forecasting.when_to_choose: Leave empty: the value that would have forecast the past best is then used.

forecasting.label: Periods kept aside for testing
forecasting.what_it_does: The last periods are hidden from the methods. Each method forecasts them, and the forecasts are compared with what really happened.
forecasting.when_to_choose: Leave empty for one full season (with fewer than three seasons of data: a fifth of the periods). Keep more aside for a harder test, fewer when the history is short.

forecasting.label: How the methods are ranked
forecasting.what_it_does: The measure of forecast error that decides which method is best on the periods kept aside.
forecasting.when_to_choose: Keep the default unless large misses are much worse for you than small ones.

options.label: Mean absolute error
options.what_it_does: The average miss, in the unit of the sales.
options.when_to_choose: Default. Easy to read: 'on average the forecast was off by this much'.

options.label: Root mean squared error
options.what_it_does: Like the average miss, but large misses count more than small ones.
options.when_to_choose: One big miss hurts more than several small ones, for example when stock runs out.

options.label: Mean absolute percentage error
options.what_it_does: The average miss as a percentage of the real sales.
options.when_to_choose: You compare products of very different size. It cannot be used when a period has zero sales.

pricing.label: Form of the demand curve
pricing.what_it_does: The shape that is fitted to the observed prices and quantities.
pricing.when_to_choose: Start with the straight line. Compare all three if you are unsure, and prefer the simplest one that fits.

options.label: Straight line
options.what_it_does: Every price step of the same size takes away the same number of units: quantity = a - b x price.
options.when_to_choose: Default. Prices were tested in a narrow range, or you want the form that is easiest to explain.

options.label: Constant elasticity
options.what_it_does: Every price rise of 1% changes the quantity by the same percentage, the elasticity: quantity = A x price^elasticity.
options.when_to_choose: You want one elasticity number to compare products or markets. Take care outside the tested prices: this curve never reaches zero and has no ceiling.

options.label: Logit
options.what_it_does: An S-shaped curve. At low prices the quantity approaches a ceiling, the market size. At high prices it approaches zero.
options.when_to_choose: Prices were tested over a wide range and the quantity levels off at the low end.

pricing.label: Market size
pricing.what_it_does: The number of units all buyers together would buy in a period. For the logit curve it is the ceiling of the curve. For a curve from the conjoint simulator it turns shares into units.
pricing.when_to_choose: Logit curve: leave empty to estimate the ceiling from the data, or enter it if you know it. Conjoint curve: leave empty to get quantities as shares in percent (market size 100).

pricing.label: Lowest allowed price
pricing.what_it_does: The search for the best price does not go below this price.
pricing.when_to_choose: A lower price would hurt the brand, or a contract sets a floor. Leave empty for no floor.

pricing.label: Highest allowed price
pricing.what_it_does: The search for the best price does not go above this price.
pricing.when_to_choose: Retailers or competitors set a ceiling, or you do not trust the curve above the tested prices. Leave empty for no ceiling.

pricing.label: Choice rule
pricing.what_it_does: Turns each respondent's utilities for the products into predicted shares.
pricing.when_to_choose: Depends on how people buy the product: by habit and variety, or one considered choice.

options.label: Share of preference (logit)
options.what_it_does: Each respondent is split across the products in proportion to e^(scale x utility). A product with a slightly higher utility gets a slightly higher share.
options.when_to_choose: Default. Everyday products that people buy often and switch between, like oat drinks.

options.label: First choice
options.what_it_does: Each respondent counts fully for the one product with the highest utility.
options.when_to_choose: Rare, considered purchases where people pick a single winner. It needs precise part-worths: with few answers per respondent, shares can be several percentage points off, and far more inside a single segment.

pricing.label: Scale
pricing.what_it_does: Used by the share of preference rule only. It sets how strongly a difference in utility turns into a difference in share. With 0 all products get the same share. The larger the scale, the closer the result comes to the first choice rule.
pricing.when_to_choose: Keep 1 unless you know real market shares. Then change the scale until the predicted shares of existing products match the real ones.

pricing.label: Target segment
pricing.what_it_does: Ranks the products by their predicted share in this one segment. Empty means all respondents.
pricing.when_to_choose: You have chosen a target segment and want the product that wins there.

targeting.label: Model
targeting.what_it_does: The method that learns from the past campaign who responds.
targeting.when_to_choose: Start with the logistic regression. Try the tree to get rules you can read aloud, and compare the two on the test sample.

options.label: Logistic regression
options.what_it_does: Gives every predictor one weight. The weights add up to a score, and the score becomes a probability of response between 0 and 1.
options.when_to_choose: Default. Each predictor pushes the chance of response steadily up or down. Usually the better ranking of customers.

options.label: Decision tree
options.what_it_does: Splits the customers again and again by one yes-or-no question about a predictor, such as 'more than 3 orders last year?'. Each final group gets its own response rate.
options.when_to_choose: You want simple rules, or you expect that predictors only matter in combination.

targeting.label: Share of customers kept aside for testing
targeting.what_it_does: This share of the customers, picked at random, is hidden from the model. The model is then judged on them. The rest is the training sample.
targeting.when_to_choose: Keep 0.3. With few customers use less, but never judge a model only on the data it learned from.

targeting.label: Seed
targeting.what_it_does: The starting number for the random split into training and test sample. The same seed gives the same split.
targeting.when_to_choose: Keep the default. Change it to see how much the results depend on the split.

targeting.label: Probability from which a customer counts as a responder
targeting.what_it_does: Used for the table of right and wrong predictions (confusion matrix) and the hit rate. A customer with a probability at or above this value is predicted to respond.
targeting.when_to_choose: 0.5 is the usual value. If few customers respond, almost nobody reaches 0.5: lower the value, or judge the model by its lift instead of its hit rate.

targeting.label: Number of groups in the gains and lift table
targeting.what_it_does: Customers are sorted from the highest to the lowest probability and cut into this many groups of equal size.
targeting.when_to_choose: Keep 10 (deciles). Use 20 for a finer view of a large list, 5 for a small one.

targeting.label: Depth of the tree
targeting.what_it_does: How many questions in a row the tree may ask before it stops.
targeting.when_to_choose: Keep 4 for a tree that fits on a page. A deeper tree follows the training sample more closely and often does worse on the test sample.

targeting.label: Smallest group of the tree
targeting.what_it_does: No final group of the tree may hold fewer training customers than this.
targeting.when_to_choose: Keep 50, so that every response rate rests on enough customers. Lower it only for small data sets.

targeting.label: Size of the list you plan to contact from
targeting.what_it_does: The profit is measured on the test sample. With this number it is scaled up to the size of your real list.
targeting.when_to_choose: Leave empty to see the profit for the test sample itself.

lifetime_value.label: When the margin is earned
lifetime_value.what_it_does: Decides when in a period the customer pays, and so which customers pay at all. Textbooks use different conventions, and they give different values for the same customer.
lifetime_value.when_to_choose: Pick the option that matches how your customers pay. State the convention whenever you report a lifetime value.

options.label: At the start of each period
options.what_it_does: The first margin is earned now, for certain. Every later margin is earned at the start of its period, from the customers who are still there. Value = margin x (1 + d) / (1 + d - r).
options.when_to_choose: Default. Customers pay in advance, as with a subscription.

options.label: At the end of each period
options.what_it_does: Every customer who starts a period pays at its end. The first margin comes one period from now. Value = margin / (1 + d - r).
options.when_to_choose: Customers pay afterwards, for example by invoice at the end of the year.

options.label: At the end of each period, from the customers who stayed
options.what_it_does: Only customers who are still there at the end of a period pay for it. Value = margin x r / (1 + d - r). Many textbooks call r / (1 + d - r) the margin multiple.
options.when_to_choose: You want the cautious textbook formula, or margins are only earned when a customer renews.

lifetime_value.label: Number of periods counted
lifetime_value.what_it_does: Only the margins of this many periods are counted. Empty means the whole relationship, however long it lasts.
lifetime_value.when_to_choose: Leave empty for the usual lifetime value. Enter 3 or 5 if your company only plans that far ahead.

lifetime_value.label: Periods listed one by one
lifetime_value.what_it_does: How many periods the result lists in detail: who is still there, and what the period adds to the value.
lifetime_value.when_to_choose: Keep 10 for a chart. It does not change the lifetime value.

allocation.label: Increase asked about in the third judgment
allocation.what_it_does: The third judgment is the sales expected when spending is raised by this share. 0.5 means 50% more than today.
allocation.when_to_choose: Keep 0.5 unless the managers were asked about another increase, for example 0.2 for 20% more.

allocation.label: What happens to the budget
allocation.what_it_does: Decides whether the whole budget must be spent.
allocation.when_to_choose: Depends on who owns the budget: is it yours to split, or yours to justify?

options.label: Spend the whole budget
options.what_it_does: Every franc of the budget is given to a unit, even if the last francs earn less than they cost.
options.when_to_choose: Default. The budget is fixed and the question is only how to split it.

options.label: Spend up to the budget
options.what_it_does: Money is only spent as long as it earns more than it costs. The rest of the budget is left over.
options.when_to_choose: You may hand money back, or you want to know whether the budget is too large.

allocation.label: Fineness of the search
allocation.what_it_does: The search first tries splits on a grid, then fine-tunes the best one. The grid has this many steps across the money that can be moved (the budget minus the lowest spending of every unit). More steps make the first stage finer and slower.
allocation.when_to_choose: Keep 1000. Raise it only if two runs with different values give clearly different splits.

portfolio.label: Lowest rating of the scale
portfolio.what_it_does: The lowest rating a factor can get. Together with the highest rating it defines where the grid is cut.
portfolio.when_to_choose: Keep 1 for the usual scale from 1 to 5. Change it if your ratings use another scale, for example 0 to 10.

portfolio.label: Highest rating of the scale
portfolio.what_it_does: The highest rating a factor can get.
portfolio.when_to_choose: Keep 5 for the usual scale from 1 to 5.

portfolio.label: Where the grid is cut
portfolio.what_it_does: Two scores that separate low from medium and medium from high, the same for both axes. A score exactly on a cut counts as the higher level.
portfolio.when_to_choose: Leave empty to cut the scale into three equal parts (2.33 and 3.67 on a scale from 1 to 5). Enter two numbers if your company uses other limits.

portfolio.label: Size of the change in the weights
portfolio.what_it_does: In the sensitivity analysis every weight is raised and lowered by up to this share. 0.2 means that a weight of 25% is tried between 20% and 30%. The weights are then scaled so that they add up to 100% again.
portfolio.when_to_choose: Keep 0.2 for the usual doubt about weights. Choose more if the managers disagree strongly about what matters.

portfolio.label: Number of random sets of weights
portfolio.what_it_does: How many sets of weights are drawn at random. For each, every unit is placed in the grid again.
portfolio.when_to_choose: Keep 1000. More draws make the shares a little more precise.

portfolio.label: Seed
portfolio.what_it_does: The starting number for the random sets of weights. The same seed gives the same result.
portfolio.when_to_choose: Keep the default. Change it to see that the result does not depend on the draws.

panel.label: Model
panel.what_it_does: Decides which differences in the data are used: those between units, those within a unit over time, or both.
panel.when_to_choose: Start with fixed effects. Compare all three if you are unsure: the comparison says which one to trust.

options.label: Pooled regression
options.what_it_does: Treats every row as a separate case. Differences between units and changes within a unit count the same.
options.when_to_choose: The units are alike, or you want the simple benchmark. If units differ for reasons that are not in the data, this model is biased.

options.label: Fixed effects
options.what_it_does: Gives every unit its own level. Only changes within a unit over time are used, so anything that is fixed for a unit, such as its location, cannot bias the result.
options.when_to_choose: Default. Units differ in ways you cannot measure, and these may be related to the predictors (a store in a rich area sells more and charges more).

options.label: Random effects
options.what_it_does: Treats the level of a unit as a random draw. Uses the changes within units and part of the differences between units, which makes the estimates more precise.
options.when_to_choose: The levels of the units are unrelated to the predictors. The Hausman test in the comparison checks this.

panel.label: Form of the equation
panel.what_it_does: Decides whether the variables enter as they are or as logarithms.
panel.when_to_choose: Log-log is the usual form for sales and marketing mix: its coefficients can be read directly as elasticities.

options.label: Log-log
options.what_it_does: The outcome and every predictor with positive values enter as logarithms. A coefficient is then an elasticity: the percentage change in the outcome for a 1% change in the predictor. Yes/no predictors (0 or 1) stay as they are.
options.when_to_choose: Default. Effects are proportional: a price rise of 10% costs the same share of sales in a small and a large store.

options.label: Linear
options.what_it_does: All variables enter as they are. A coefficient is the change in the outcome for one more unit of the predictor.
options.when_to_choose: Effects are a fixed number of units, or a variable has zeros or negative values and cannot be put in logarithms.

panel.label: Carry-over rate
panel.what_it_does: Only used when a carry-over variable is named. The share of the effect of one period that is still there in the next: with 0.6, advertising of this week counts 60% next week and 36% the week after.
panel.when_to_choose: Leave empty to estimate the rate from the data. Enter a number if you know it from earlier studies.

sentiment.label: Words like "not" in front of a sentiment word
sentiment.what_it_does: Decides what happens to a positive or negative word that follows a negation such as "not", "never" or "isn't".
sentiment.when_to_choose: Keep the default. Switch it off to see how many reviews change, which shows how much a simple word count can miss.

options.label: Turn the meaning around
options.what_it_does: "Not good" counts as negative and "not bad" as positive. A negation reaches the next three words, but not beyond the next comma or full stop.
options.when_to_choose: Default. Negations are common in reviews, and ignoring them gives wrong labels.

options.label: Ignore negations
options.what_it_does: Every word counts as it stands: "not good" counts as positive.
options.when_to_choose: Only to show the difference, or for texts in which negations are written in a way the engine does not know.

sentiment.label: Width of "neutral"
sentiment.what_it_does: The score of a review runs from -1 (only negative words) to +1 (only positive words). Reviews with a score between minus and plus this value are called neutral.
sentiment.when_to_choose: Keep 0 to call a review positive as soon as positive words are in the majority. Raise it, for example to 0.2, if mixed reviews should count as neutral.

sentiment.label: Very common words
sentiment.what_it_does: Decides whether words such as "the", "and" or "is" are counted.
sentiment.when_to_choose: Remove them: they are the most frequent words in any text and say nothing about its content.

options.label: Leave them out
options.what_it_does: A built-in list of about 180 very common English words is left out of the counts.
options.when_to_choose: Default, for English texts.

options.label: Count them
options.what_it_does: Every word is counted.
options.when_to_choose: Texts in another language (the built-in list is English), or when you want to see everything.

sentiment.label: Shortest word that is counted
sentiment.what_it_does: Words with fewer letters than this are left out of the counts.
sentiment.when_to_choose: Keep 3. Short words are mostly fillers. Lower it if short words matter in your texts ("ok", brand names).

sentiment.label: Number of words listed
sentiment.what_it_does: How many of the most frequent words are returned.
sentiment.when_to_choose: 50 fill a word cloud well. Take fewer for a bar chart.

sentiment.label: Fewest reviews a word must appear in
sentiment.what_it_does: A word is only examined as a driver if at least this many positive and negative reviews together contain it.
sentiment.when_to_choose: Keep 20. With fewer reviews behind it, what a word seems to do is mostly chance. Lower it for small data sets.

sentiment.label: Number of drivers listed
sentiment.what_it_does: How many words are listed on the positive side and on the negative side.
sentiment.when_to_choose: 10 on each side are easy to read. All examined words are counted in the result either way.

sentiment.label: Rating from which a review counts as positive
sentiment.what_it_does: Only used when a rating column is given. Reviews with this rating or more are the positive ones.
sentiment.when_to_choose: 4 for ratings from 1 to 5 stars. Change it for another scale.

sentiment.label: Rating up to which a review counts as negative
sentiment.what_it_does: Only used when a rating column is given. Reviews with this rating or less are the negative ones. Ratings in between are left out.
sentiment.when_to_choose: 2 for ratings from 1 to 5 stars. Change it for another scale.

network.label: What makes a member an influencer
network.what_it_does: Decides by which measure of importance the members are ranked.
network.when_to_choose: Start with the number of ties. It is the simplest measure, and in the validation of this engine it gave the seeds with the widest reach.

options.label: Degree
options.what_it_does: Ranks by the number of direct contacts.
options.when_to_choose: Default. A member with many contacts tells many people directly.

options.label: Betweenness
options.what_it_does: Ranks by how often a member lies on the shortest way between two others.
options.when_to_choose: You want the message to cross from one group to another.

options.label: Closeness
options.what_it_does: Ranks by how few steps a member needs to reach everybody else.
options.when_to_choose: You want the message to reach the whole network quickly from one starting point.

options.label: Eigenvector centrality
options.what_it_does: Ranks by ties to members who are well connected themselves.
options.when_to_choose: You look for members in the core of the network. In a network with several communities this measure mostly describes the largest one.

options.label: All four measures together
options.what_it_does: For each of the four measures the members are put in order. The score of a member is the average of its four places, from 0 (last in all) to 1 (first in all).
options.when_to_choose: You want members who are strong on every count, and no single measure to decide alone.

network.label: How the seeds are chosen
network.what_it_does: Seeds are the members who are approached first. This decides whether they are simply the best ranked members, or spread over the communities.
network.when_to_choose: Spread them if the network has communities: the best ranked members often sit in the same community and reach the same people.

options.label: Spread over the communities
options.what_it_does: The largest community gets its best ranked member as a seed, then the second largest, and so on. When every community has a seed, the next best members follow.
options.when_to_choose: Default. The seeds then reach different parts of the network.

options.label: The best ranked members
options.what_it_does: The seeds are the members at the top of the ranking, wherever they sit.
options.when_to_choose: The network is one tight group, or you only care about one part of it.

network.label: Number of seeds
network.what_it_does: How many members are proposed as the first to approach.
network.when_to_choose: As many as you can afford to approach. With communities, at least one per community is a good start.

network.label: Number of members listed
network.what_it_does: How many members are listed at the top of a ranking.
network.when_to_choose: 10 are easy to read. The full table of all members is in the result either way.

network.label: Size of the communities
network.what_it_does: Steers how fine the split into communities is. Above 1 the search prefers more and smaller communities, below 1 fewer and larger ones.
network.when_to_choose: Keep 1, the standard. Change it only if the communities found are clearly too coarse or too fine for your purpose.

network.label: Random seed
network.what_it_does: The search for communities goes through the members in a random order. The seed fixes that order, so the same data gives the same communities.
network.when_to_choose: Keep it. Try another seed to see whether the communities stay the same: if they change a lot, they are not clear-cut.
